Who handles a Kentucky property tax bill

Four local offices each take one stage. Each stage has its own desk. The property valuation administrator (PVA) puts the value on every parcel. Fall bills come from the sheriff, who also takes the payments. Whatever is still open after April lands with the county clerk, then the county attorney follows up on it.

The PVA aims for fair cash value, which is what a willing buyer and seller would agree on. Each parcel gets a physical review at least every four years, and new construction is added annually. Farmland may be valued as agricultural land. Coal, oil, gas and utility property go to the state Office of Property Valuation instead.

So call the PVA about value, the sheriff about what you owe now, and the clerk about anything that has slipped past April 15. That avoids a lot of phone tag once a sale is underway.

How to contest your assessment

Your first move is a conference with the PVA or a deputy, which can happen by phone on request. If you still disagree afterward, hand the clerk a brief written petition that names the parcel, your reasons and the value you believe is fair.

The roll goes on public display the first Monday in May for 13 days. File no later than the end of the next workday after the display closes. A PVA can request more time, and with state approval the deadline can move out by up to 25 days. Skip the local board, or miss your own hearing, and you lose the later state appeal.

  • The local board of assessment appeals meets 25 to 35 days after the roll closes, with a public hearing on every protest.
  • Proof wins these cases: recent sale or listing prices, building costs, insurance policies, mortgages or loans. A protest backed by nothing must be denied.
  • You may make an audio recording of your hearing.
  • If you hire someone to speak for you, they must hold a role the statute names, such as lawyer, CPA, tax consultant, real estate broker or appraiser, or be your employee, and you must authorize them in writing.

An appeal never freezes the bill. KRS 133.120(9) has you pay based on the value you put in your petition. Should the final value come out higher, the gap plus interest is yours to pay. When bills print before an appeal ends, your claimed value is used and a second bill covers anything the board adds.

Write down what you saw when you walked the property: peeling roof, a cracked foundation, a dated kitchen. Photos and repair quotes carry real weight at a hearing, and the same file helps you explain your asking price to a buyer.

If you lose at the county board

Further review goes to the state tax appeals board under KRS 49.220. It must receive your petition within 30 days after the county board mailed its decision. That board decides the matter anew instead of reading the earlier record.

Any time the county board changes a value it must explain why in writing, and if you or the PVA request it, the board has to visit the parcel. KRS 133.120 was amended in 2026, so read the current wording before you file.

The Kentucky tax calendar

This is the standard schedule. A county that mails bills after November 1 runs a later version, with a 30 day window for each stage.

Standard Kentucky real property schedule
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Valuation snapshot date
Jan. 1 to Mar. 1Owners may list real property
Early May (first Monday)Roll on display for 13 days
Oct. 1 to Nov. 1Early payers save 2%
Nov. 2 to Dec. 31Face amount due
All of January5% added
Feb. 1 to Apr. 1521% added
End of day Apr. 15Unpaid bills leave the sheriff for the clerk

Listing is not an annual chore when last year's roll described your land and buildings completely and accurately and nothing big has changed.

For a homeowner planning a spring listing, the practical dates are early October and the turn of the year. Paying in October trims the bill and leaves a clean record for the buyer's title search, while waiting until January means a surcharge that a closing agent will expect to see paid off at the table.

Who sets the tax rate?

Every taxing body chooses its own rate, within House Bill 44. It may drop to the compensating rate, which holds revenue from existing property level. It may also pick a rate that grows that revenue by at most 4 percent, after a public hearing. Anything higher invites a voter petition and a possible recall vote. Rates are written as cents per $100 of value.

The state's own 2025 real property rate, announced by the Department of Revenue, is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value, lower than the 10.9 of the year before. State revenue growth from existing property is capped at 4 percent. Cities, school districts, counties and special districts each layer on a rate of their own, so what you pay depends on the parcel's address.

What happens when a bill goes unpaid

Once April 15 passes, your unpaid bill turns into a certificate of delinquency, which is a lien on the parcel. Costs then stack up stage by stage.

  • Interest accrues at 1 percent a month.
  • The clerk adds a 10 percent fee and the attorney adds 20 percent, though the attorney's portion is waived for an owner who pays within five business days after the clerk receives the list.
  • Notices come from the county attorney, one by May 15 and another by June 15, with payment plan offers included.
  • Certificate sales to private buyers start in mid-July and can continue into late October, though most wrap up by the end of August.

The thing sold is the lien, not the house. You remain the owner, but the investor now holds the debt and adds fees of its own.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentucky houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed or due

Know your balance before you put a sign in the yard. Ask the sheriff what the current bill is, and ask the clerk whether any certificate of delinquency is attached to the parcel. A county has to publish its delinquent list online and in the newspaper at least 30 days ahead of a sale.

As the seller you also owe the real estate transfer tax of $0.50 per $500 of declared value, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded. Foreclosure transfers and surrenders in lieu of foreclosure are outside it. A homestead exemption on the property should be reported to the PVA at transfer. Organizations with a Section 170 exemption, such as churches or libraries, use Revenue Form 62A023.

The title company will search for any open delinquency and pay it out of your proceeds. A cash buyer purchasing as-is follows the same path, with the unpaid balance coming off what you receive, so an early number keeps closing on time.

Pull together the latest bill, a payoff figure from the sheriff or clerk, and the assessed value on file. Set that value beside recent nearby sales. If it looks too high while the display window is open, a free conference with the PVA could lower it for the next owner as well.

Frequently asked questions

When does a Kentucky property tax bill arrive and when is it due?

Bills go out from the sheriff in the fall, and collection opens October 1 or November 1 depending on the county. Pay through November 1 for a 2 percent discount. Face value is accepted through December 31.

Until what day can I protest my valuation?

File one workday after the 13 day display period closes. Display begins the first Monday in May, and you need to meet with the PVA first.

What penalties hit a late Kentucky bill?

All of January adds 5 percent. From February 1 to April 15 the add-on is 21 percent. After that the clerk takes over and 1 percent monthly interest and more fees apply.

Can the county sell my home over unpaid tax?

The sale covers the lien, a certificate of delinquency, not the house. You keep title but owe whoever bought the certificate.

Who fixes the state real property rate?

The Department of Revenue, each year by July 1 under KRS 132.020. The 2025 figure is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value.

Kentucky homestead exemption

This is a deduction from the assessed value of a Kentucky home for owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Section 170 of the Kentucky Constitution created it, and the deduction is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. Property tax is then figured on whatever value is left.

The reduction applies to state, county, city and special district taxes alike, so it lowers the whole bill and not just one line of it.

Who qualifies

Two things have to be true at once: an age or disability test, and a residence test. KRS 132.810 sets both.

  • The applicant is 65 or older during the year of the application, or was classified as totally disabled on January 1 of that year under a federal agency program or a retirement system inside or outside Kentucky.
  • The applicant owns the property and maintains it as a personal residence.
  • A disabled applicant has received disability payments and keeps the classification for the whole taxation period.
  • Only one exemption is allowed per residential unit, even when two residents both qualify.

Ownership can take several forms. Legal or equitable title, joint tenancy, tenancy in common, a condominium and certain corporate or leasehold interests of more than 98 years all count. A mobile home, an RV classified as real property or a manufactured house qualifies as a residential unit.

How and when to apply

File with the property valuation administrator, the PVA, in the county where the home sits. Applications are due by December 31 of the eligible tax year and can be submitted online, by mail or in person, depending on what the local PVA office accepts. Phone the office to learn which method it prefers.

An applicant based on age can prove it with a birth certificate, driver's license, passport or other approved document. A disability applicant needs proof of the classification. The state form is titled Application for Exemption Under the Homestead/Disability Amendment.

The valuation you write on the form cannot be used to raise your assessment. If it is, the statute requires an adjustment the next year so that your total tax comes out the same as if the increase never happened.

If the tax bill is already paid, or still unpaid

Timing decides whether you get a reduced bill or a refund. If you qualify before paying the bill for that year, you are entitled to a full or partial exoneration that reflects the exemption. If you qualify after paying, you are entitled to a refund of the tax on the exempt portion of the value.

Heirs and late-year sellers should pay attention here. A seller who is eligible but never applied can ask the PVA whether an application for the current taxation period is still possible before the December 31 deadline, and can ask the sheriff how the bill would be adjusted.

How the exemption amount changes

The $6,500 written into Section 170 is read as $6,500 in 1972 purchasing power. Every two years, if the federal cost of living index has moved at least 1 percent, the Department of Revenue adjusts the maximum. The 2025 and 2026 figure is $2,750 higher than the 2023 and 2024 figure.

Kentucky homestead exemption maximums (KRS 132.810)
PeriodMaximum exemption
Section 170 original amount (1972 dollars)$6,500
2023 and 2024 assessment years$46,350
2025 and 2026 assessment years$49,100

The amount is recalculated every second year. Ask your PVA for the figure that applies to the tax year you are working with, since a later two-year period will carry a different number.

When you sell or inherit the home

The exemption belongs to the owner, not to the house. When title to an exempt property passes, the owner, administrator, executor, trustee, guardian, conservator or agent has to report the transfer to the PVA. A buyer or an heir who is 65 or disabled has to file a fresh application of their own.

A death also ends the period. If the person holding the classification dies before December 31, the taxation period runs only from January 1 to the date of death. A disabled owner who stops meeting the total disability classification must tell the PVA, and the exemption ends at the close of that taxation period without being prorated.

The exemption has no effect on the deed tax. The grantor still pays fifty cents per $500 of value at recording, unless the transfer falls in one of the listed exceptions such as a foreclosure or a transfer between spouses.

Checklist for a seller with the exemption

A few quick checks keep the paperwork clean when a house with an exemption changes hands.

  • Ask the PVA to confirm the exemption is on file for the current year and which person it is tied to.
  • Ask the sheriff for the current bill so you can see whether the exempt value was already applied.
  • Tell the PVA about the transfer once the deed is recorded, since the statute requires the owner or the estate's representative to report it.
  • If the owner has died, keep the date of death handy, because it caps the taxation period for that year.

Tell the buyer the deduction will not carry over automatically. A younger buyer will simply see a bill computed on the full assessment, so the first tax bill after closing can be noticeably higher than the one you paid.

Do disabled owners under 65 have to reapply every year?

Usually yes. A totally disabled owner under 65 must apply annually. Two groups are excused after documenting the disability at the first application: totally disabled former members of the Armed Forces with a service-connected disability, and people found totally and permanently disabled under Social Security rules, Kentucky Retirement Systems rules or another provision of the Kentucky Revised Statutes.

Missing an annual renewal can cost a year of savings, so mark December 31 on the calendar if you are in this group.

Creditor protection is a separate homestead rule

KRS 427.060 exempts an individual debtor's interest of up to $5,000 in the home the debtor or a dependent uses as a permanent residence, or in a burial plot, from sale under execution, attachment or judgment. It does not apply to foreclose a mortgage given by the owner or for purchase money, and it does not reach debts that existed before the property was bought or improved.

That $5,000 figure is far lower than the tax exemption, and the two are unrelated. The tax deduction lowers a bill. The creditor protection limits what a judgment creditor can take.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Other exempt property under Section 170

The same section lets Kentucky exempt property held by government, institutions of education, religious institutions, public libraries, cemeteries not run for private profit and institutions of purely public charity. Those owners file Revenue Form 62A023 with the PVA, who may forward unclear cases to the department. The homestead deduction for seniors and disabled owners is a different benefit with its own form.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Kentucky homestead exemption?

It is $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years. That amount comes off the assessed value of the home, and tax is figured on the rest.

What age do I have to be to claim it?

You must be 65 or older during the year you apply, or be classified as totally disabled. You also have to own the home and use it as your personal residence.

Where do I file the application?

File with the property valuation administrator in the county where the home is located. Applications are due by December 31 of the tax year.

Does the exemption transfer to the person who buys my house?

No. It follows the owner. You must report the transfer to the PVA, and a buyer or heir who is 65 or disabled needs to apply on their own.

Can I get money back if I qualified after paying my taxes?

Yes. KRS 132.810 entitles an applicant who qualifies after the bill is paid to a refund of the tax tied to the exempt value.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Kentucky has an inheritance tax, not an estate tax

Kentucky taxes what an heir receives, not the estate as a whole. The inheritance tax falls on a beneficiary's right to receive property from a deceased person, and the amount depends on the beneficiary's relationship to the decedent and the value received.

Closer relatives get larger exemptions and lower rates. All property of a Kentucky resident is subject to the tax except real estate located in another state. Real estate and personal property in Kentucky owned by a nonresident can also be taxed, which matters when an out-of-state owner leaves a Kentucky house to heirs.

Which heirs owe tax, and at what rates

Only Class B and Class C beneficiaries owe tax, and the rates run up to 16 percent. KRS 140.070 sorts every recipient into one of three classes.

Kentucky beneficiary classes (KRS 140.070 and 140.080)
ClassWho is in itRate rangeExemption
ASurviving spouse, parent, child by blood, stepchild, adopted child, grandchild through those children, nephew, niece, brother, sisterNo taxTotal inheritable interest
BSon-in-law, daughter-in-law, aunt, uncle, qualifying great-grandchild4 percent to 16 percent$1,000
CAny other person, plus institutions such as religious or educational bodies6 percent to 16 percent$500

Nieces and nephews sit in Class A under the current statute text. The 2026 amendments to KRS 140.070 and 140.080 apply to estates of people who died on or after January 1, 2026.

How the Class B and Class C brackets work

The tax is progressive within each class, so only the slice of value inside a bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate. Class B starts at 4 percent on the first $10,000 and rises through 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 14 percent to 16 percent on value above $200,000. Class C starts at 6 percent on the first $10,000 and reaches 16 percent on value above $60,000.

Because Class C rates start two points higher and climb faster, a distant relative or a friend pays noticeably more on the same inheritance than a Class B heir does. The exemption is charged against the lowest brackets first.

  • A surviving spouse's interest can include a qualifying trust or life estate if the personal representative makes the election on the Department of Revenue form by the return due date.
  • For a nonresident decedent, the exemption is prorated by the share of property Kentucky can tax.

Return and payment deadlines

For a death on or after July 1, 2026, the return and the payment are due within 24 months of death. A five percent discount applies if the tax is paid within 14 months, and no interest runs if payment arrives inside the 24 months.

  • Deaths before July 1, 2026: 18 months to file and pay, with the five percent discount for payment inside 9 months.
  • Deaths on or after July 1, 2026: 24 months to file and pay, with the five percent discount for payment inside 14 months.
  • After the deadline, interest runs at the tax interest rate defined in KRS 131.010 until the Department of Revenue is paid.
  • If the tax is not paid by the deadline, the personal representative or trustee must give bond for the tax and interest.

A return is required when a federal estate tax return is required and the estate has property Kentucky can reach. It is also required when any asset passes to a beneficiary taxable under KRS 140.070. The personal representative computes the tax, or the beneficiaries do if no representative serves.

Paying in installments

When a beneficiary's net tax is more than $5,000, the beneficiary may elect to pay in 10 equal annual installments. The first installment is due with the return and the rest follow one year apart.

The election must be written, signed by the beneficiary and filed with the Department of Revenue when the estate return is filed. Interest on the deferred portion starts 24 months after death for a death on or after July 1, 2026, and 18 months after death for earlier deaths. A beneficiary who elects to defer stays personally liable for the unpaid balance.

2026 changes for recent deaths

Two sets of amendments took effect in the spring of 2026, and each has its own start rule. They change the class list and the clock, so an old guide may give the wrong answer for a recent death.

  • KRS 140.070 and 140.080 were amended effective April 27, 2026, and apply to estates of people who died on or after January 1, 2026.
  • KRS 140.160, 140.210 and 140.222 were amended effective April 14, 2026, and set the 24-month and 14-month periods for deaths on or after July 1, 2026.
  • For a death before July 1, 2026, the 18-month return and payment date and the 9-month discount period still govern.

Pin down the exact date of death before you plan the sale. A death on June 30 and a death on July 1 of the same year sit under different clocks.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentucky houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling an inherited Kentucky house

Heirs who owe the tax often sell the house to fund it, so the filing deadline should drive the listing date. A Class A heir owes nothing, which leaves the timing to probate and the heirs' own plans. A Class B or Class C heir should work out the bill early, because the 14-month discount for a death on or after July 1, 2026 can save five percent of the tax.

Before closing, ask the Kentucky Department of Revenue's inheritance tax staff whether the file shows any open balance or lien on the property, and ask the title company what it needs from the estate. Keep the personal representative's letters, the date-of-death value support and the deed handy, since the buyer's title agent will ask for them.

  • List the heirs and note each one's class from KRS 140.070.
  • Estimate the tax for every Class B or C heir using the brackets above.
  • Decide whether proceeds will pay the tax at closing or after distribution.

How long the state can collect

The Department of Revenue generally has ten years from when the cause of action first accrued to sue to collect. That clock is suspended when an estate is delayed by litigation or another unavoidable cause, and it is suspended during any deferred payment period an heir has elected.

A fraudulent return has no time limit, because the tax can be assessed and collected at any time. Heirs who sell early and distribute everything should keep tax records for the full ten years, since the personal representative and, in a deferral, the beneficiary may be asked about unpaid amounts.

Frequently asked questions

Does Kentucky have an estate tax?

No. Kentucky has no estate tax. It taxes the heir's right to receive property instead, through the inheritance tax in KRS Chapter 140.

Does a child or spouse owe Kentucky inheritance tax on an inherited house?

No. A surviving spouse, child, parent, grandchild, sibling, niece and nephew fall in Class A, and Class A beneficiaries are exempt on their total inheritable interest.

How long do heirs have to pay Kentucky inheritance tax after a 2026 death?

For a death on or after July 1, 2026, the tax is payable within 24 months, with a five percent discount if paid within 14 months. Earlier deaths keep the 18-month and 9-month periods.

Can the inheritance tax be paid over time?

Yes, when a beneficiary's net tax exceeds $5,000 the beneficiary can elect 10 equal annual installments. The election is filed in writing with the return, and the first installment is due then.

Does Kentucky tax a Kentucky house owned by someone who lived elsewhere?

Yes. Real estate and personal property located in Kentucky and owned by a nonresident can be taxed, and the exemption is prorated for a nonresident decedent.

How a Kentucky eviction case works

Kentucky calls an eviction lawsuit a forcible detainer action, and it starts in District Court in the county that holds the rental. Under KRS 383.200, a tenant's refusal to hand back possession after the term ends counts as a forcible detainer. Under KRS 383.210 the court answers a landlord's complaint with a warrant to the sheriff or a constable.

Self-help is off the table. The case moves through the court from filing to the order that returns the house to the owner, and changing locks or cutting services along the way runs into KRS 383.690.

Steps from complaint to possession

The statutes set the order of events. Several steps carry short deadlines, so a landlord who has the paperwork ready before filing saves weeks.

Forcible detainer steps under KRS 383.200 to 383.285
StepWhat happens
Complaint (KRS 383.210)Landlord files in District Court and a warrant goes to the sheriff or a constable
Service (KRS 383.210, 383.215)Each defendant gets notice of the time and place at least three days ahead; without notice, no inquiry proceeds against that defendant
Trial (KRS 383.210(2))The court tries the case unless a party demands a jury
Judgment (KRS 383.240)Restitution of the premises and costs for the landlord, or costs for the defendants
Appeal window (KRS 383.255)Seven days after the finding
Warrant of restitution (KRS 383.245)If no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues the warrant on request

The seven-day appeal and the rent deposit

Whoever loses can appeal within seven days after the finding. An appellant has to place the rent owed since the case began, plus every later month's rent as it falls due, with the circuit court clerk.

The money stays with the clerk until the court orders it paid out when the appeal ends. Making that deposit perfects the appeal, which pauses the inquisition and sends the file up to circuit court within ten days. An appellant who drops the appeal, along with any surety, answers under KRS 383.260 for the landlord's losses from the delay and the reasonable cost of defending the appeal.

Preparing for the hearing

Bring paper that proves the tenancy and the default. A landlord's file should hold the lease, the rent ledger, any termination notice with proof of delivery, and photographs if damage is claimed. A tenant's file should hold rent receipts, repair requests and any written agreement about late payments.

  • Either party can ask the court to issue subpoenas for witnesses, and the court can compel attendance under KRS 383.230.
  • A defendant served less than three days before the hearing can move to adjourn until the three days have run, under KRS 383.215.
  • A jury is used only if a party demands one, and the sheriff does not summon one unless a party gives written notice of the demand.

What if the occupant was never a tenant?

KRS 383.290, enacted in 2025, lets an owner ask a law enforcement officer to remove a person who is in the house without permission, but only when every condition fits. A current or former tenant, or anyone who once had the owner's agreement to live there, cannot be removed this way.

  • The person has never been a tenant and never held a written or oral agreement from the owner.
  • The building was closed to the public on the day the person came in.
  • The owner has told the person to go.
  • The person is outside the statute's list of close relatives, and no lawsuit over the property is pending between the two sides.

The owner hands the officer a signed petition, the officer checks identification and serves a notice to vacate, and a sheriff or constable may charge a $20 service fee. Someone wrongfully removed has 60 days to sue in District Court and can win lawyer fees, so reserve this route for clear cases.

What speeds a case up, and what is off limits

Prompt filing, service on every named occupant and complete records move a case fastest. Pulling doors, changing locks or shutting off utilities does the opposite, because KRS 383.690 bars taking possession that way.

  • Think before taking rent once a termination notice is out. KRS 383.675 treats acceptance with knowledge of a default as a waiver of that breach.
  • Avoid rent hikes or threats right after a tenant's code complaint. KRS 383.705 presumes retaliation when the complaint came within the year before.
  • After termination, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent plus a separate claim for actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3).
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentucky houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Time limits for filing

KRS 383.285 bars an inquisition of forcible entry or detainer more than two years after the entry or detainer complained of. That is the outer limit, and the practical window is far shorter.

Where the URLTA has not been adopted, KRS 383.160 lets a landlord retake a house without demand or notice if the case begins within 90 days after a term of a year or longer ends, or within 30 days after a shorter term ends. Miss those windows and the next chance comes later, so file soon after a lease runs out.

Costs and damages a landlord can recover

The judgment for the landlord restores possession and awards the costs of the case. KRS 383.240 states the form: restitution of the premises plus costs expended, or costs for the defendants if they prevail.

Money claims are separate. After a termination under the URLTA, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant's willful noncompliance can support actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3). Keep rent ledgers, repair invoices and photographs so those amounts can be proved at trial.

A pending eviction and the sale of the house

A pending case does not block a closing, but it decides who has to deliver the keys. Judgment alone does not empty the house, because possession arrives with the warrant of restitution.

Buyers and lenders often want a vacant house, so the contract should name who finishes the case, who pays its costs and what happens if the tenant appeals and the deposit sits with the clerk. Ask the closing attorney how the seller's duties to the tenant are handled once title passes.

  • Get the case number, judgment and any warrant of restitution into the sale file.
  • Confirm whether any rent is sitting with the circuit court clerk after an appeal.
  • Ask the title company whether the occupancy affects the closing date.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Court forms and where to get help

Call the clerk's office at the District Court for the house's county and ask for the current forcible detainer forms and filing fee. The Kentucky Court of Justice also runs a Legal Self-Help section on its website.

A real estate attorney can confirm which notice rules apply in your city and how a pending case should be handled in the sale contract. Ask the clerk, too, how the court wants service on each occupant arranged with the sheriff's office.

Frequently asked questions

Which court handles evictions in Kentucky?

The District Court for the county where the rental stands. The landlord files a forcible detainer complaint, and a warrant then goes to the sheriff or a constable under KRS 383.210.

What is the deadline to appeal a Kentucky eviction judgment?

Seven days after the court's finding. The party who appeals must also deposit the unpaid rent and each later month's rent with the circuit court clerk.

Can an owner change the locks or shut off power to remove a tenant?

No. KRS 383.690 forbids regaining the dwelling by cutting heat, electricity, water, gas or another essential service. The court order is the only route.

Does a sheriff remove a tenant after the judgment?

Yes. If no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues a warrant of restitution on request, which directs the sheriff or constable to put the landlord in possession.

Can I use the quick removal process for a former tenant?

No. KRS 383.290 excludes current and former tenants and anyone who once had the owner's agreement to live there. Those disputes go through forcible detainer.

content:
Kentucky Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Quitclaim Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What a quitclaim deed passes on

A quitclaim deed gives the buyer or relative whatever the signer owns in the parcel, and promises nothing about how solid that ownership is. The McCracken County Clerk describes it as a deed that works by release: it passes any title or claim the grantor may have, with no warranty or covenants for title.

Kentucky gives warranty deeds their own wording. Under KRS 382.030, the words 'with general warranty' become a promise to defend the property against all persons, and KRS 382.040 narrows that promise to claims made by or through the grantor. A quitclaim carries neither promise.

That is why quitclaims turn up between relatives, former spouses and co-heirs, and in cleanups of an old record. A buyer paying full price usually wants more than a quitclaim in the chain. If you plan to resell afterward, mention the quitclaim to the closing agent early so the title search can allow for it.

  • It conveys the grantor's interest, large or small, as it stands on the day of signing.
  • It does not create ownership the grantor never had.
  • It does not remove a mortgage, a judgment lien or an unpaid tax lien from the parcel.

What the deed must contain to be recorded

KRS 382.135(1) sets out what every deed to real property needs, and a quitclaim counts as a deed for this purpose. The clerk cannot accept a deed that falls short, so a missing line means a rejected filing and a second trip to the courthouse.

  • Full name and mailing address of both the grantor and the grantee.
  • A statement of the full consideration.
  • An in-care-of address where the tax bill for the transfer year can be sent.
  • A sworn, notarized certificate signed by both sides. It either confirms the consideration or states that the transfer is a gift and gives the estimated fair cash value.

Two more statutes add to the list. KRS 382.335 calls for a signed statement naming whoever prepared the deed, with that person's address, plus the grantee's mailing address. KRS 382.110 wants the deed to point back to the grantor's source of title: book and page if the title came by recorded deed, or a plain account of how and from whom it arrived if it came by inheritance. Under KRS 382.130, a deed made in Kentucky can go to record on the maker's acknowledgment before the clerk or a notary.

Where to record it and what it costs

File with the county clerk where the land lies. If a parcel straddles a county line, use the county that holds the larger share. KRS 382.110(1) sets that rule. Fees come from KRS 64.012 and the transfer tax from KRS 142.050.

Kentucky charges for recording a deed
ChargeAmount
Recording and indexing, up to 5 pages$33, of which $27 stays with the clerk and $6 goes to the affordable housing trust fund
Each page after the fifth$3
Each added reference to the same instrument$4
Permanent records storage reimbursement$10 under KRS 64.012(3)(a)
Real estate transfer tax, paid by the grantor$0.50 for each $500 of value or fraction of $500

Counties post their own totals. McCracken County's clerk publishes a $50 deed filing fee with the same $3 charge for pages past five. Phone the clerk where your parcel sits and get the all-in number before you drive over.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kentucky house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When transfer tax applies

KRS 142.050 puts the tax on the grantor, and the clerk collects it before taking the deed. On a sale it is figured on the full consideration, liens included. On a gift, or when the deed shows a token price, the statute substitutes the estimated open-market value. The clerk does the math, which is why a deed that understates the price draws questions.

Subsection (7) lists the exempt transfers. These are the ones a quitclaim most often involves:

  • Parent to child, or grandparent to grandchild, for a token price only.
  • One spouse to the other, or between former spouses in a divorce.
  • A deed that only confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed.
  • A transfer made solely to secure or release a debt.
  • Partition, foreclosure, or a voluntary surrender in lieu of foreclosure.
  • A trustee to a successor trustee, and certain moves into a trust whose only beneficiary is the grantor.

An exemption waives the tax, not the paperwork. A gift deed from mother to daughter still needs the notarized fair cash value certificate under KRS 382.135 even though no tax is owed.

If the grantor inherited the property

A deed from someone who took title by descent needs one extra document. Under KRS 382.120, the grantor, any heir at law, or two Kentucky residents with personal knowledge must give the clerk an affidavit before the deed is filed. It names the person who died, the date of death, whether that person was married, where they lived and that they died without a will, and it lists each heir with age, address, relationship and share.

The clerk records the affidavit, indexes it under the ancestor as grantor and each heir as grantee, and charges the same fees as for a deed. KRS 382.135(4) adds a duty for estates passing by will or intestacy: before the estate closes, the personal representative files an affidavit in each county where land lies, naming who receives each parcel and its estimated value. Heirs quitclaiming to one another to consolidate a family house should make sure both affidavits are on file first, since the clerk will not take the deed ahead of them.

Penalties for a false statement on a deed

KRS 382.990 attaches criminal penalties to deed paperwork. Willfully and fraudulently giving a false statement of the full actual consideration, or of the full estimated value, under KRS 382.135 is a Class D felony. Knowingly swearing to a false statement in the descent affidavit under KRS 382.120 is a Class A misdemeanor, and the person is liable to anyone injured by its use.

Write the true figure. If a family member is paying a token amount for a house worth far more, say so on the deed and let the clerk compute tax on market value or apply the parent and child exemption. Shaving a few dollars off transfer tax by understating the price leaves a recorded document that can be challenged later, and a future buyer's title company will read it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentucky houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does a quitclaim help when you plan to sell?

Sometimes. It can put the title into the right names so a sale can close, and it can also cause delay. A quitclaim leaves every lien and tax debt in place. KRS 382.070 adds a warning: a seller who leaves part of the price unpaid has no lien against creditors and purchasers unless the deed states what remains unpaid.

Owners who inherited a Kentucky house, fell behind on payments or hold a property with repair problems often ask whether a quitclaim to a relative will simplify things. The better first step is usually a payoff request to the lender and to the county for any unpaid tax, then a plain talk with a closing attorney. If you want a direct cash sale of a Kentucky house as it stands, a quitclaim signed beforehand does not change what the buyer's title company has to clear.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a lawyer to record a Kentucky quitclaim deed?

No statute requires one, but KRS 382.335 makes the deed show the name and address of the person who prepared it. Many people use an attorney or title company so the consideration certificate, source of title and legal description are right on the first filing.

Is a notary required on a quitclaim deed in Kentucky?

Yes. The grantor's signature must be acknowledged, and KRS 382.135 requires the consideration or gift certificate to be sworn and notarized by both sides. County clerk offices can notarize for a fee set in KRS 64.012, so ask the clerk before you sign anywhere else.

What does recording a Kentucky quitclaim deed cost?

State law sets $33 for up to five pages and $3 per extra page, and KRS 64.012 also allows a $10 records reimbursement. Transfer tax is fifty cents per $500 of value unless an exemption fits. McCracken County's clerk posts a $50 deed fee, so confirm the figure with the clerk who will record yours.

Can I quitclaim my house to my child and avoid transfer tax?

A transfer between parent and child for only a token price is exempt under KRS 142.050(7)(l). The deed still needs the sworn certificate that calls it a gift and states the estimated fair cash value.

Which office records a Kentucky quitclaim deed?

The county clerk where the property, or most of it, sits. A deed recorded in the wrong county fails to put later purchasers and creditors on notice, which is the protection the grantee needs.

title: Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed: How It Works
content:
Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed: How It Works

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Transfer on Death Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Kentucky has no transfer on death deed

As things stand, no statute authorizes one. KRS Chapter 391, the chapter on descent and distribution, has no transfer on death deed sections. Lawmakers have tried more than once, but the bills stalled before they reached the governor.

In 2024, House Bill 50 proposed a Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act and was sent back to the House Appropriations and Revenue Committee. In 2026, Senate Bill 34 proposed a similar act and went to the House Local Government Committee. Neither became law. An owner who records a document labeled a transfer on death deed in Kentucky is relying on a form the statutes do not provide for.

Because the legislature may return to the subject, check the bill pages on the legislature's website before you rely on any summary, this one included.

What Senate Bill 34 would have changed

The bill summary on the General Assembly's site is a preview of what a Kentucky version could look like, and a reminder that it would have come with strings.

  • The deed would not be a lifetime transfer. Ownership would pass at the transferor's death, and the transferor could revoke it at any time.
  • It would be nontestamentary, so it would not need to meet the formalities of a will.
  • It would have to be recorded before the transferor's death, and a floor amendment would have voided a deed filed too late.
  • Any later deed transferring an interest in the same property would revoke the earlier transfer on death deed.
  • The Department of Revenue would supply the forms, the state Medicaid agency would supply a form about any Medicaid lien, and KRS 64.012 would be amended to set a recording fee.
  • The same bill would have created a beneficiary designation for motor vehicle titles.

None of that is law. The amendments show the details were still moving when the bill stopped.

When the owner dies without a will

KRS 391.010 sets the order of inheritance, and it was amended by 2026 Acts chapter 134. The surviving spouse comes first. Children and their descendants come next, then parents, siblings, grandparents, and then aunts, uncles and stepchildren. If no kindred exist, the property vests in the state under KRS 393.020.

Surviving spouse's share of intestate real estate, KRS 391.010(1)(a)
Who survives the ownerSpouse's share
No descendantsThe entirety
Descendants, all of them also descendants of the spouseThe entirety
Descendants who are not lineal descendants of the spouseOne-half
Shared descendants, plus a spouse with other descendants of their ownOne-half

Whatever the spouse does not take passes to the next group in that order. A family that wants a different result for one house needs a will, a trust or a lifetime deed, since a deed that takes effect at death is not available as a statutory tool.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kentucky house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Options instead of a transfer on death deed

Kentucky owners work with the tools the statutes do recognize. None is a perfect substitute, and each has tradeoffs worth talking through with an estate attorney before you sign.

  • A will. It passes the house to the person you name, but the estate usually goes through probate before a deed can be signed.
  • A deed with survivorship wording. KRS 381.120 sends a joint tenant's share to that person's heirs or devisees, so survivorship has to be written into the instrument. KRS 381.130(1) carves out an estate conveyed to persons when it manifestly appears from the instrument that the share of the one who dies should belong to the others.
  • A lifetime deed, with or without a retained life estate. It moves title now, so recording costs and the new owner's rights start immediately.
  • A trust. KRS 142.050(8) exempts certain transfers to and from a trustee from the transfer tax, including one where the grantor is the sole beneficiary.

KRS 391.360 treats written provisions for a nonprobate transfer in a trust, conveyance or deed of gift as nontestamentary, and leaves creditors' rights alone. Whether a given document does what its signer hopes is a job for an attorney, not a printed form.

Changing a survivorship deed

A joint tenant can partition their share during life. Under KRS 381.130(2), one or more joint tenants may partition their interest by a deed or other instrument that states the intent to partition and is recorded with the county clerk where the land lies. The partition takes effect on recording and turns that tenant's interest into a tenancy in common.

One exception protects couples. Residential property owned only by a husband and wife as joint tenants with right of survivorship, and occupied by them as a principal residence, cannot be partitioned this way. For everyone else, a survivorship deed lasts only as long as the co-owners leave it alone. A parent who adds a child to a deed to avoid probate also hands that child a present interest in the house.

What heirs file before selling an inherited house

Two affidavits come up again and again. KRS 382.135(4) requires the personal representative of an estate that passes by will or intestacy to file an affidavit with the county clerk of each county where property lies, naming each recipient with an address and giving the full or fair market value used for estate purposes. KRS 382.120 requires an affidavit of descent before a deed from an heir is filed, setting out the ancestor's name, date of death, marital status, residence, the fact of intestacy and each heir's relationship and share.

With those in order, the deed itself must follow KRS 382.135(1) and KRS 382.335: full names and mailing addresses, a statement of consideration, an in-care-of address for the tax bill, the notarized certificate, the signed preparer statement and a reference to the source of title. For a house coming out of an estate, the source statement describes how and from whom the heirs obtained it.

Heirs who want a quick sale should start gathering these papers right away. A cash buyer can close fast once the clerk's records show who holds title, but the closing cannot get ahead of the filings.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kentucky houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Fees and tax on a lifetime deed

A lifetime deed to a family member is a deed like any other. KRS 142.050(7)(l) exempts a transfer between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, made for only nominal consideration, and a gift deed still needs the notarized certificate stating the estimated fair cash value. The clerk's fee under KRS 64.012 is $33 for up to five pages, plus $3 for each page after that.

Before recording any deed in a parent's name, ask the county clerk what that office will accept, and ask an attorney how the transfer affects the owner's own security. Giving up control during life is a much bigger step than signing a document that would only take effect at death.

Frequently asked questions

Can I record a transfer on death deed in Kentucky?

No statute authorizes one. KRS Chapter 391 has no transfer on death deed sections, and the 2024 and 2026 bills proposing one did not become law. Ask an estate attorney which authorized instrument fits your goal.

What happens to my house in Kentucky if I die without a will?

It descends under KRS 391.010. A surviving spouse takes all the real estate when the decedent had no descendants or when all descendants are shared with the spouse, and one-half when some are not the spouse's. The rest follows the statutory order of kin.

Is joint ownership with a child a safe way to avoid probate?

It carries risk. Survivorship must appear in the deed, a joint tenant can partition their share by recorded deed under KRS 381.130, and the child becomes a present co-owner during your life. Speak with an attorney first.

Will Kentucky pass a transfer on death deed law soon?

Nothing in the statutes points that way. Senate Bill 34 of 2026 and House Bill 50 of 2024 both stalled in committee. Bill status is public on the legislature's website.

Can heirs sell an inherited Kentucky house quickly?

Yes, once the estate paperwork is in place. The personal representative's affidavit under KRS 382.135(4) and any affidavit of descent under KRS 382.120 must be on file with the county clerk, and the deed has to meet the content rules before it will be recorded.

title: Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House
content:
Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Kentucky
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Kentucky Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Kentucky House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Kentucky?
We buy Kentucky houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Kentucky tax house sale profit separately?

No. Kentucky has no capital gains schedule. KRS 141.020 levies one flat percentage on the entire net income of a resident, so profit from a Kentucky closing simply joins the rest of that year's income.

With a flat state rate, the big variable for a Kentucky seller is how much profit is left after the federal rules apply. A longtime homeowner may shield nearly all of it. A landlord, a flipper or an heir who sells an inherited house usually cannot. Ask the Kentucky Department of Revenue how an excluded gain is carried onto Form 740 before you file.

Kentucky income tax rate by year

A closing in a taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 2026 is taxed at 3.5 percent of net income. The rate has stepped down several times, so the year of the closing matters.

Kentucky individual income tax rate by taxable year (KRS 141.020)
Taxable years beginningRate on net income
2018 through 20225 percent
20234.5 percent
2024 and 20254 percent
2026 and after3.5 percent

Further cuts for 2027 and later years depend on budget triggers and a vote of the General Assembly. The statute bars the department from lowering the rate by itself, so do not count on a lower rate when you pick a closing date.

The federal main-home shield

Federal law lets a seller shield up to $250,000 of profit on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return. Two tests apply, and both are measured over the five years that end on the closing date.

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for two years or more.
  • Use: you lived there as a residence for two years or more. On a joint return, each spouse must meet this test personally.
  • The two-year spans can fall at different points inside the five-year window.
  • A seller who shielded profit on a different home during the two years before this closing generally cannot claim it again.
  • Members of the Uniformed Services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community on qualified extended duty may freeze the five-year window for as long as a decade.

A Form 1099-S from the closing agent creates a duty to report the sale even if no tax is due. Reporting is also required whenever part of the profit is left over after the shield.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kentucky house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Figuring your profit

Profit is the net amount you realize at closing minus your adjusted basis. Basis begins with the purchase price plus sales tax and buying costs. It rises with improvements that add value and falls with depreciation claimed and insurance money received for casualty or theft losses.

If you put a new roof or a finished basement into a Kentucky house, keep those invoices. Each one lifts basis and trims the taxable profit. An heir or a recipient of a gift follows different basis rules, explained in IRS Publication 551. A house held for one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed like wages, while a longer hold produces long-term gain.

A loss on a home you lived in cannot be deducted. A sale below basis gives no write-off.

Federal tax on profit above the shield

Long-term profit lands in one of three federal tiers, zero, fifteen or twenty percent, set by taxable income and filing status. The cutoffs are republished each year in IRS Topic no. 409, so read the table for your closing year instead of trusting an old figure.

Depreciation changes the picture for rentals. The slice of profit that reflects depreciation on real property (unrecaptured section 1250 gain) can be taxed at up to 25 percent federally. Reporting runs through Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Rentals and inherited houses

A house you never lived in fails the use test, so the main-home shield is generally unavailable. Depreciation you took reduces basis and raises profit, and a rental that has run for years can produce a large number even when the market barely moved.

An inherited house raises two separate questions. One is income tax on profit above basis, which follows Publication 551. The other is Kentucky inheritance tax, a levy on the heir's right to receive property under KRS Chapter 140 that has nothing to do with your Form 740. Class A heirs, such as a spouse, child or sibling, are exempt from that second tax.

  • Pull depreciation schedules before listing, not after closing.
  • Ask the estate's personal representative for the valuation papers used on the estate return.
  • Choose a closing date with the tax year and its rate in mind.

Timing the sale

Because the rate depends on the taxable year, a closing in late December and one in early January can land in different years. Look at your other income for each year, any credits you rely on and the date the two-year use test is met. If you are a few weeks short of two years in the home, waiting can turn a taxable gain into a shielded one. Talk to a tax preparer before signing a contract with a firm closing date.

Sellers who live outside Kentucky or moved during the year

A nonresident owes Kentucky tax on income from tangible property in Kentucky, and a house here counts as that property. KRS 141.020 also taxes a part-year resident as a resident for the months of residency and as a nonresident for the remaining months.

The Department of Revenue prints Form 740 and Form 740-NP. Ask the department which return fits your move date, because that choice decides whether the whole profit or only the Kentucky-sourced part is reported.

Credits a large sale can affect

Kentucky offers a $40 credit for each person aged 65 or over and for a legally blind individual, and a $20 credit for Kentucky National Guard members. A nonrefundable family size tax credit under KRS 141.066 is tied to modified gross income and family size, with a 2025 ceiling of $42,760.

A closing can lift modified gross income for the year, so a household that normally qualifies for the family size credit may lose it in a sale year. Run the numbers with the closing profit included before you decide on the sale date.

Papers to gather before closing

Collect the records that fix basis and residency now, because the closing agent's Form 1099-S shows only the sale price. A short list saves a preparer hours later.

  • The closing statement from your own purchase, showing cost and buying expenses.
  • Receipts for work that added value, such as a roof, an addition or a finished basement.
  • Depreciation schedules if any part of the house produced rent.
  • Proof of the dates you lived there, such as utility bills and the address on your license.
  • For an inherited house, the estate valuation papers and the personal representative's letters.

A taxable profit may call for estimated tax payments during the year. Ask the Department of Revenue whether Kentucky estimated payments apply to your sale year, and set aside part of the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

Does Kentucky give a break for selling a main home?

Kentucky has no home sale break of its own. The federal shield of $250,000 single or $500,000 joint controls how much profit you have, so confirm with the Department of Revenue how it appears on Form 740.

What rate will Kentucky charge on my profit for a 2026 closing?

The rate is 3.5 percent of net income for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the same percentage that applies to wages.

Do I report the sale if the whole profit is shielded?

Yes, when you receive a Form 1099-S or when any portion of the profit is left over. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D where they apply.

Can I write off a loss on a house I lived in?

No. Losses on personal-use property such as a home are not deductible.

Does someone who lives in another state owe Kentucky tax on selling a Kentucky house?

Yes. Kentucky taxes a nonresident's income from tangible property in the state. Ask the department which return applies and how credits are prorated.
